clue.text: Bargain King Richard put up front

indicators.note: the name is placed at the front, ahead of the royal letters

parts.note: Dick is the familiar short form of the name Richard
ER, Edward Rex, is the royal cipher of a King Edward

explanation.surface: A monarch called Richard is shoved into the vanguard to strike a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: ER usually means the Queen (Elizabeth Regina), but it equally stands for Edward Rex, so 'King' can give it.
explanation.definitionFit: To dicker is to haggle, so it is a verb synonym for bargaining over a price.

clue.text: Fighters putting end to quarrel in fitting arena

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the run of the other two words

parts.note: due means fitting or proper
the lists were the arena for jousting

indicators.note: the end of the word quarrel is its final letter

explanation.surface: Combatants bring a dispute to an end in a suitable ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lists' is the old name for a tournament ground; 'putting' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Duellists are people who fight a formal duel, so they are combatants.

clue.text: Providing familiar friend with sound support could be a feather in one's cap

definitions.text: could be a feather in one's cap

parts.note: cock is familiar British address for a mate, as in 'wotcher, cock'

indicators.note: sound means said aloud, so the word for support is heard, not spelt

parts.note: aid is support

explanation.surface: Giving a close mate a bit of reliable help could be a feather in one's cap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like reliable; it signals the homophone. 'Cock' is chummy British slang for a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A cockade is a rosette or knot of ribbon worn on a hat, much as a feather might be.

clue.text: Some self-indulgence of a little imp

indicators.note: some of means only part of the run of letters is used

explanation.surface: A small sprite shows a measure of self-indulgence.
explanation.definitionFit: Elfin means like an elf, the small mischievous creature of folklore.

clue.text: One thus in charge covering staff division under constant pressure

indicators.note: the letters for one, thus and in charge wrap around the division, enclosing it

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
thus means so
a bar line divides a musical staff into bars

explanation.surface: Someone in authority oversees a section of employees while under steady strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like employees, but it is the musical stave, which bar lines divide.
explanation.definitionFit: An isobaric process in physics takes place with no change in pressure, the term built from Greek for equal weight.

clue.text: Bound by conservative tendency in annual purification ritual?

parts.note: a bound is a spring or leap
a leaning is a tendency

explanation.surface: Conservative instincts tie a person to a yearly cleansing rite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' reads as tied, but it is a leap.
explanation.definitionFit: Spring-cleaning is the thorough clean of a house done each year, jokingly a ritual of purification.

clue.text: See old penalty reduced after mistake

indicators.note: the old and penalty pieces come after the word for mistake

parts.note: bish is British slang for a blunder

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: the price of something is the penalty paid for it

explanation.surface: Look at an ancient fine cut down after an error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like an imperative verb; it is a bishop's diocese. 'Bish' is British schoolboy slang for a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is a bishop's diocese or office, the same thing as a bishopric.

clue.text: Lifting a bit of corn in combine

indicators.note: the head of grain is put inside the word for combine

parts.note: a ring is a group of traders combining to fix prices
an ear is the grain-bearing head of a cereal stalk

explanation.surface: A combine harvester raises a bit of corn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'combine' suggests the farm machine; it is a business cartel or ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearing means raising up, as a horse rears by lifting its forelegs.

clue.text: Desert transport arrived and left

parts.note: came means arrived

explanation.surface: A vehicle for the Sahara turned up and then departed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like departed; it is the abbreviation L.
explanation.definitionFit: The camel is the traditional beast of burden for crossing deserts.

clue.text: Be persuaded by powerful speaker with a line so movingly put across

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are placed across, on either side of, the loud speaker
the letters are moved about into a fresh order

parts.note: Stentor was the Greek herald in the Iliad with a voice of fifty men

explanation.surface: A loud orator stirringly delivers a phrase that wins people over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'powerful speaker' is no adjective-and-noun: Stentor was the Homeric herald whose voice is the root of 'stentorian'; 'put across' means the jumble straddles him.
explanation.definitionFit: To listen to reason is to accept sensible argument, being talked round.

clue.text: Top chef in English officers' mess

indicators.note: a mess is a muddle, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A celebrated cook works in the officers' dining mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess' pretends to be the military dining room; it signals the anagram of E and OFFICERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Escoffier was the famous French chef who codified modern haute cuisine.

clue.text: Quarters provided by a jolly host

parts.note: south and west are two quarters of the compass
a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM

explanation.surface: Lodgings are laid on by a cheerful landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'host' reads as a landlord, but it means a multitude; 'jolly' is crossword slang for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: A host is a great crowd, as is a swarm of people or insects.

clue.text: Memorise line and get ready

parts.note: ready is slang for cash, so to get readies is to earn

explanation.surface: An actor commits a line to memory and prepares to go on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get ready' looks like preparing; 'ready' is British slang for money, so getting it is earning.
explanation.definitionFit: To learn a speech is to commit it to memory.

clue.text: Operating thus in test of shock treatment?

indicators.note: the two short words sit inside the word for test

parts.note: a trial is a test
a machine that is operating is on
thus means so

explanation.surface: Something is working this way during a trial of electroconvulsive therapy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shock' suggests electric shocks, but it is a shock of hair, whose treatment is the barber's work.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonsorial means relating to barbers and hairdressing, the treating of a head of hair.

clue.text: Carriage for rest of the passengers

definitions.text: Carriage for rest of the passengers

parts.words: Carriage for rest of the passengers
parts.note: a railway carriage fitted with berths so travellers can sleep overnight; 'rest' reads like the remainder of the passengers

explanation.definitionFit: A railway coach with bunks is where travellers take their rest on a night train.

clue.text: Expert around court applauded

indicators.note: the word for applauded goes around the court letters

parts.note: praised means applauded

explanation.surface: A skilled player on the tennis court received applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expert' is an adjective, skilled.
explanation.definitionFit: Practised means skilled through long experience, so expert.

clue.text: Monarch abandoning seed pearl, for example

indicators.note: the monarch's letter leaves the word for seed, which goes on without it

parts.note: a germ is a seed or embryo
R, for rex or regina, stands for a monarch

explanation.surface: A king throws away a seed pearl, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seed pearl' looks like one phrase; 'seed' belongs to the wordplay and 'pearl' to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pearl is an example of a precious stone or jewel.

clue.text: Motorway's hazard producing accident

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written MI with the 's
a hazard is a chance or risk

explanation.surface: Hazards on the motorway cause a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds; its 1 is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A mischance is a piece of bad luck, an unlucky mishap.

clue.text: Unfortunate expulsion of odd characters from islands

indicators.note: the letters in odd positions are thrown out of the word, leaving the even ones

explanation.surface: Unlucky eccentrics are deported from some islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd characters' sounds like eccentric people; it means letters 1, 3, 5 and 7, removed to leave S, A, D.
explanation.definitionFit: Sad can mean regrettable or deplorable, as in a sad state of affairs.

clue.text: Disaster as vehicle taken over by new driver goes into river

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the river's name

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland

indicators.note: in a down clue over means turned upside down, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a cab is a vehicle
L is the learner plate on a novice driver's car

explanation.surface: A crash happens when a car driven by a learner ends up in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken over' sounds like a hijack; it reverses CAB to BAC.
explanation.definitionFit: A debacle is a sudden collapse or complete fiasco.

clue.text: Youngsters making fuss — not so much to pocket money

parts.note: ado is a fuss

indicators.note: the word for not so much takes the coin into its pocket, holding it inside

parts.note: less means not so much
a cent is a small coin

explanation.surface: Teenagers make a fuss about getting less pocket money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to pocket' looks part of the phrase 'pocket money'; in fact the small coin is pocketed by the word for not so much.
explanation.definitionFit: Adolescents are young people in their teens, between childhood and adulthood.

clue.text: What man may wear for deadly sort of American party

definitions.meaning: an item of men's clothing knotted at the collar
old American slang for a lynching, the rope being the neckwear

explanation.surface: A dark joke about what to wear to a fatal gathering in the States.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie for the neck is menswear, and a lynch mob's hanging was grimly called a party of that kind.

clue.text: We beg to differ, taking points to mediator

indicators.note: to differ is to be unlike, so these letters take on a different order

parts.note: east and north are compass points

explanation.surface: Someone politely disagrees while making a point to an arbitrator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We beg to differ' reads as a polite idiom; its first three words are the anagram fodder, signalled by 'differ'.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-between carries messages between parties, acting as an intermediary.

clue.text: Prepare for riding habit

definitions.meaning: to mount a horse is to climb on to it
a habit is an outfit, like a riding habit

explanation.surface: Get ready to go out on horseback in a proper outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting up on to a horse means mounting it, and an outfit or costume is a get-up.

clue.text: Bookmaker's account accepted by that fellow backing

indicators.note: backing means the combined letters are read in reverse
the account letters are taken inside the pronoun

parts.note: that fellow is him

explanation.surface: A turf accountant's account is taken by that man, who is betting on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bookmaker' is a turf accountant in the surface but means the writer of a book of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: The prophet is traditionally the author of a book of the Old Testament named after him.

clue.text: Runner — one obviously pleased if given second start

indicators.note: the runner, given the extra letter at its start, would become the word for one pleased

parts.note: a smiler is someone visibly pleased

explanation.surface: An athlete is clearly happy to be given a second start.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse device: add S at the start of the runner and you have the pleased one, so the answer is SMILER without its S.
explanation.definitionFit: A miler is an athlete who races over a mile.

clue.text: Changes of direction taking toll, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is spoken, so the word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a toll is a tax or levy

explanation.surface: Route switches impose a charge, it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'toll' might suggest a bell; it is a levy.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailing ship tacks when it turns into the wind to change course, so tacks are course changes.

clue.text: One in isolation has to divulge information repeatedly

parts.note: to sing is criminal slang for informing
to let on is to reveal a secret

explanation.surface: A person in solitary confinement must keep confessing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repeatedly' tells you the phrase 'divulge information' is used twice, giving two different synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: A singleton is a single individual or item, standing alone rather than in a pair or group.

clue.text: Piano playing first is appealing

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
leading is going first in a game, as in playing the first card

explanation.surface: A pianist who opens the recital is attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appealing' looks like attractive but means making an appeal or plea.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleading is begging earnestly, the same as appealing to someone.

clue.text: It sounds like the fat of the land

indicators.note: the clue says outright that the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: grease is animal fat

explanation.surface: The phrase 'the fat of the land' is heard, meaning luxury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the fat of the land' is an idiom for plenty; 'the land' alone is the definition, a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Greece is a country, a land in south-east Europe.
